A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mutual-evaluation framework, renamed from LLM-Crowdsourced to League of LLMs. All nine pages of v1 and 21 pages of v3 are readable, including figures, tables, equations and v3 Appendices A–G. v1 has no appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments evaluating eight LLMs on generated mathematics and programming questions, including performance plots, ranking consistency and observed answering errors.

after.justification: v3 reports original five-run experiments in both domains, with performance summaries, uncertainty estimates, family-score comparisons and external-ranking analyses.

M1.justification: The four-phase pipeline, rotating questioner, independent answering, reference-based mutual evaluation, self-evaluation exclusion and score aggregation remain unchanged. v3 explicitly names Borda scoring and supplies fuller prompts, but these disclosures do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: The task experiments retain dynamically generated mathematics and ACM-style programming questions, the same eight model versions and unrestricted programming-language choice. v3 compares external benchmark rankings but does not report evaluating additional task instances from those benchmarks.

E2.justification: v3 Section 6 and Figure 5 introduce explicit ranking comparisons with MATH500, AIME2024, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval and mathematics/coding Chatbot Arena leaderboards. v1 only asserts agreement with unspecified mainstream benchmarks and Chatbot Arena, without corresponding comparator-specific results. The eight mutually evaluated LLMs remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds secondary-analysis protocols using leaderboard snapshots for Spearman correlations and pooled in-family versus out-of-family scores. Appendix D describes Top-k overlap across independent runs, whereas v1 discusses agreement among evaluators, limiting direct comparability of that statistic. The primary question-generation and evaluation design is retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds developer-family scoring-bias analysis and quantitative external-ranking validation, and extends consistency analysis across k = 1–7. Appendix F expands the existing Dirichlet-series case with reference and erroneous answers. Conversely, v1's programming illustrations involving quantum path counting and the Cube Garden solution are removed.

E5.justification: The reported independent runs increase from three to five. v3 newly supplies score and Top-k confidence intervals, across-run standard deviations, ANOVA and Tukey comparisons, Welch tests for family-score differences, and significance reporting for ranking correlations; v1 lacks these formal statistical reports.

E6.justification: Results and rankings change substantially: programming o3-mini moves from 53.8 and last place in v1 Figure 6 to 79.5 and second in v3 Figure 4. These are different three-run and five-run summaries, not demonstrated same-setting gains. Reported memorization cases change from 10/168 to 22/280, and Top-k consistency from 74.85% to 70.7%. v3 also adds concrete benchmark correlations and family-score differences.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix F, Figure 9 adds an abridged mathematical derivation for the retained Dirichlet-series example, covering convergence, a functional identity and an expression for F(0). v1 presents the question without this worked reference solution. Neither version develops formal guarantees for the evaluation framework.

C1.justification: v3 elevates OpenAI-family homophily to a headline empirical contribution, replacing the abstract's emphasis on Gemini's superior question generation. It also narrows broad claims about overcoming existing evaluation limitations and generalizability, positioning LOL as a complement and specifying internal ranking stability.

C2.justification: The programming interpretation reverses from consistency between solving and question-setting abilities to their decoupling. v3 proposes shared architecture, training data or styles as possible explanations for homophily. Its new limitations address correlated evaluator errors, open-ended tasks, restricted task/model coverage, human validation, API cost and scaling overhead.

D1.justification: Appendix G provides answering and evaluation prompts absent from v1 and expands the question-generation templates, including JSON formats and the mathematics answer-length constraint. v3 also specifies temperature 1, default remaining parameters, the Borda point mapping and independent validation by at least three annotators. These are additional disclosures, not established changes to existing settings.

R1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated comparison with LLM-as-a-Judge, citing Zheng et al. and Pan et al., and connects its design to evaluator-bias research such as Liu et al. and Ye et al. This substantially sharpens positioning against the closest research. The earlier broad survey is condensed, including removal of benchmark-saturation discussion and associated citations.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites and condenses retained introductory, motivational, methodological and experimental prose. It renames the framework, introduces numbered sections, separates Related Work, Discussion and Limitations, and organizes supporting material into Appendices A–G.

P2.justification: The conceptual and pipeline figures are largely retained, while performance plots are reordered and recaptioned. The two original prompt figures become expanded appendix displays. v3 adds six tables, benchmark-correlation and evaluator–responder heatmaps, and case-study panels, alongside substantial changes to typesetting and figure placement.

improvement.justification: v1's reliability claims rely largely on qualitative discussion and one Top-k statistic. v3 adds inspectable score summaries, uncertainty analyses and explicit external-ranking comparisons, supplies missing prompts, and acknowledges substantive limitations. These substantially improve evidential support and reproducibility. A material caveat remains: Appendix E compares different responder groups without capability controls, so its score differences support the headline homophily interpretation less securely than claimed.
